claim: A fire with heavy smoke — orange flames at the base feeding a churning grey smoke column rising above.

q1_defects.answer: Nothing broken, misaligned, cut off, or glitchy. All four captures show a coherent composition: bright orange flame mound at the base, red transition zone, grey smoke column above, all with soft organic edges. No slab/shelf banding, no tile/lattice grid, no mirror seam, no jagged edges visible in any frame. The flat horizontal floor at the bottom of the flame is the shared capture-viewport floor (identical in the fire-flame ground-truth play-2 frame), not a clip defect. bandingScore runs 0.396-0.468, above the 0.25 nominal threshold, but the known-good fire-flame ground truth scores 0.427-0.491 on the same metric — it is inflated by the intense bright-flame-to-black vertical gradient on fire tiles, and visual inspection of every frame confirms no discrete shelves or stacked-card structure. Zero console and network errors.
evidence: metrics: play-2 bandingScore=0.434 vs fire-flame ground-truth play-2 bandingScore=0.491 (known-good baseline is HIGHER → score inflated by flame/black gradient, no visible shelves)

q2_reads_as.answer: Yes — it reads exactly as claimed: 'orange flames at the base feeding a churning grey smoke column rising above.' Every play frame shows precisely that structure: a white-hot/orange flame mound at the bottom, a red ember transition, and a desaturating grey smoke column rising and dissipating at the top. Dominant warm hue 28-36 deg at sat 0.27-0.35 across play frames sits squarely in fire's band (10-45 deg) and is actually MORE saturated than the fire-flame ground truth (hue 37-43 deg, sat 0.17-0.27). warmFrac 0.73-0.79, coolFrac 0, magentaFrac 0 — no pink ring, no cream/olive drift, no ACES warm-to-cool shift. The grey of the smoke column is correct desaturation for smoke, not a hue error.
evidence: metrics: play-1 effHue=36 effSat=0.35 warmFrac=0.79 coolFrac=0 magentaFrac=0 — in fire band, more saturated than ground-truth fire-flame play-1 (hue 43, sat 0.25)

q3_discoverable.answer: Yes. All three labeled controls do exactly what their names promise, visibly and sensibly, across their ranges. smokeAmount low removes the smoke column entirely (pure flame mound) and high produces a tall thick grey column — a first-time user sliding it sees an immediate, obvious cause-and-effect. rise low gives a short stubby column while high stretches and thins it upward. turbulence low gives a smooth laminar blurred cone, high gives a violently churning, detailed flame — exactly what a non-technical user would expect those words to mean. All three sweeps report changed=true in metrics.
evidence: control: rise/smokeAmount/turbulence all changed=true; smokeAmount low→high satPixels 2377→1786 with column appearing, meanLuma 28.5→35.5

q4_responsive.answer: Responsive. The three play frames show real, continuous motion — flame lobes and smoke billows visibly reshape between play-1, play-2, and play-3 — with frameDeltaMag 4.39 / 5.14 / 6.10, larger deltas than the ground-truth fire-flame (2.69-5.53). Control apply latency is consistent at 576-597 ms across all nine sweep captures — a perceptible but sub-second beat, uniform across controls, with no dead or stuck sweeps.
evidence: metrics: frameDeltaMag play-1=4.39 play-2=5.14 play-3=6.10; control latencyMs 576-597 across all 9 sweep frames

q5_net.answer: PLEASED. 'That looks like a real campfire pumping out smoke — the flames glow white-hot at the bottom, the smoke is properly grey and churns as it rises, and when I drag the smoke slider the smoke actually goes away or thickens. It looks like movie footage, not a video game.' Smooth, organic, photoreal-grade volume on the trusted webgpu backend with zero errors.
evidence: metrics: backend=webgpu, consoleErrors=[], all 3 controls changed=true

flags.note: bandingScore (0.396-0.468) exceeds the 0.25 nominal visibility threshold on every frame, but the known-good fire-flame ground truth scores 0.427-0.491 on the same metric and visual inspection shows no slab/shelf/lattice structure — the metric appears inflated by the bright-flame-to-black gradient on fire-family tiles. Worth recalibrating the metric for fire tiles, not a visual defect.
